extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and jurors in U.S. patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions covering infringement (direct, indirect, foreign supply), willfulness, and validity (burden, written description, enablement, best mode, prior art/anticipation) in U.S. patent cases. Intended to guide judges in instructing juries and to clarify legal elements and standards of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducement (indirect infringement) — knowledge and specific intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Inducement requires that the alleged infringer knowingly induced infringement and possessed specific intent to encourage another’s infringement. The mere fact that an alleged infringer knew or should have known there was a substantial risk that another’s acts would infringe is not sufficient for active inducement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee notes incorporate the "willful blindness" standard from Global-Tech; where willful blindness is not at issue, language should be omitted to avoid juror confusion. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(b); Global‑Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., Muniauction, Lucent, DSU Med., MGM Grokster, Insituform, Ferguson Beauregard, Warner‑Lambert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful blindness standard for inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where willful blindness is implicated, the instruction should incorporate the Supreme Court's willful‑blindness standard (Global‑Tech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee: include willful blindness language only where patentee proceeds on that theory; omission advised otherwise to reduce juror confusion. See Global‑Tech Appliances v. SEB S.A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement — five elements
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for contributory infringement if the patent holder proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) [alleged infringer] sells, offers to sell, or imports within the United States a component of a product, or apparatus for use in a process, during the time the patent is in force; (2) the component or apparatus has no substantial, noninfringing use; (3) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) [alleged infringer] is aware of the patent and knows that the products or processes for which the component has no other substantial use may be covered by a claim of the patent or may satisfy a claim under the doctrine of equivalents; and (5) that use directly infringes the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each requirement must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(c); Aro; Ricoh; Alloc; Mentor; Hewlett‑Packard; Preemption Devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 271(f)(1) — supply of components from U.S. for combination abroad (active inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove § 271(f)(1) liability (active inducement of foreign combination), patentee must prove by a preponderance that: (1) accused supplies (or causes to be supplied) components from the United States to a place outside the United States that make up all or a substantial portion of the invention of any claim; (2) accused takes action intentionally to cause another outside the United States to assemble the components; (3) accused knows of the patent and knows the encouraged acts constitute infringement; and (4) the encouraged acts would constitute direct infringement if carried out in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accused believed the acts would not constitute infringement in the U.S. or that the patent was invalid, cannot be liable for inducement. Instruction should address willful‑blindness only when that theory is asserted. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f); Cardiac Pacemakers; Microsoft v. AT&T; Liquid Dynamics; Pellegrini; NTP; Union Carbide; Waymark.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 271(f)(2) — supply of components from U.S. for combination abroad (contributory foreign infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove § 271(f)(2) liability, patentee must prove by a preponderance that: (1) accused supplies (or causes to be supplied) a component from the United States to a place outside the United States; (2) the only substantial use for the component is in a product that would infringe the patent if the combination had occurred in the United States; (3) accused is aware of the patent and knows the component has no other substantial use and may be covered by a claim of the patent (literally or under doctrine of equivalents); and (4) accused intends for the component to be used in a product that would directly infringe the claim if used in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities and commentary similar to §271(f) generally; statute cited is 35 U.S.C. §271(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: § 271(g) — sale/import/use in U.S. of product made abroad by patented process
rubrics_metrics.description: Accused is liable for direct infringement if patent holder proves by a preponderance that accused, without authorization, imports, offers to sell, sells, or uses within the United States a product made outside the United States by a process that, if performed in the United States, would infringe the claim literally or under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if the product has been materially changed by an additional process or has become a trivial and nonessential component of another product, there is no infringement. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §271(g); Bayer v. Housey; Ajinomoto v. ADM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement where one or more system components located outside the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement requires that the accused system include every element recited in the claim. If some (but not all) elements are located outside the United States, the patent holder must prove by a preponderance that the control of the system was exercised and the benefit of the system was enjoyed in the United States (i.e., the place where the system as a whole is put into service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on place where control is exercised and beneficial use obtained. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §271(a); NTP v. Research in Motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement by combined acts of multiple parties — control/direction rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no single party performs all steps of a claimed process but multiple parties collectively perform every step, the claim is directly infringed if one party has control over the entire accused process so that all steps are attributable to the controlling or directing party. Mere arms‑length cooperation is insufficient; the accused must control or direct the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holder must prove by a preponderance (1) all steps were performed in the U.S. and (2) accused has control over or directs the other(s) so that steps are attributable to accused. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §271(a); Muniauction; BMC Resources; On Demand Machine; Cross Med.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limelight / Akamai principal — no inducement without direct infringement by single entity
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Limelight Networks v. Akamai, there can be no induced‑infringement liability where no single entity is liable for direct infringement under §271(a); i.e., where there has been no direct infringement, there can be no inducement under §271(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several instructions (previously on divided performance/collective inducement) have been removed in light of Limelight (U.S. Supreme Court remand and ruling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — two‑part recklessness test and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness requires patent holder to prove by clear and convincing evidence that accused acted recklessly. The test has two parts: (1) Objective: accused acted despite a high likelihood that its actions infringed a valid and enforceable patent (the objective prong is evaluated without regard to accused’s state of mind; legitimate defenses show lack of recklessness). (2) Subjective: if objective prong satisfied, patent holder must prove accused actually knew or should have known that its actions posed an unjustifiably high risk of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine subjective state of mind, jury may consider nonexhaustive factors including: (1) whether accused acted in accordance with industry standards; (2) intentional copying of patentee’s product; (3) whether there was a reasonable basis to believe accused did not infringe or had a reasonable defense; (4) good‑faith efforts to avoid infringement (e.g., design around); (5) attempts to cover up infringement. If accused relies on an opinion of counsel, instruct jury to evaluate whether the opinion was of sufficient quality that reliance was reasonable. Burden is clear and convincing evidence. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §284; In re Seagate; Knorr‑Bremse; Crystal Semiconductor; WMS Gaming; Read; Gustafson. Committee note: objective recklessness determination may be a question of law for the judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that any claim of a patent is invalid, alleged infringer must persuade the factfinder by clear and convincing evidence, i.e., leave the factfinder with a clear conviction that the claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are presumed valid under 35 U.S.C. §282. Invalidity may be asserted for failure to comply with 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112, or 251. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §282; Microsoft v. i4i; Schumer; Buildex; Hybritech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent's specification must contain an adequate written description of the invention. Alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails the written description requirement. The requirement is satisfied if a person having ordinary skill in the art, reading the original application, would recognize that it describes the full scope of the claimed invention as finally claimed and that the inventor actually possessed that full scope by the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description can be met by any combination of words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, etc., in the application. The full scope need not be expressly disclosed if a person of ordinary skill would understand it to be present. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §112; Ariad (en banc); Lizard Tech; Univ. of Rochester; Chiron; Purdue; Lampi; Gentry; Regents of Univ. of Cal.; In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must contain a sufficiently full and clear description of how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention so that a person having ordinary skill in the art could do so at the time of filing without undue experimentation. Failure to enable renders a claim invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors for determining undue experimentation (Wands factors) include: (1) time and cost of necessary experimentation; (2) how routine experimentation is in the field; (3) whether patent discloses specific working examples; (4) amount of guidance in the patent; (5) nature and predictability of the field; (6) level of ordinary skill in the field; (7) scope of the claimed invention. No single factor is dispositive; weigh all evidence in context. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §112 ¶1; Sitrick; Auto. Techs.; AK Steel; Union Pac.; Ajinomoto; In re Wands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that the specification does not disclose what the inventor believed to be the best way to make/use/carry out the claimed invention at the time of the original filing. The best mode requirement is claim‑by‑claim and focuses on inventor's subjective belief at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two questions: (1) did inventor believe there was a best way at the time of filing? (2) does the patent describe what inventor believed to be the best way with enough detail to enable a person of ordinary skill to carry it out without undue experimentation? Patent may disclose other modes and need not label which is best. Note: under the America Invents Act (effective Sept. 16, 2011), failure to disclose best mode is no longer a basis for invalidity/enforceability (statutory change). Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §112 ¶1; Pfizer v. Teva; Bayer v. Schein; Bruning; Glaxo; Transco; Wahl; Chemcast; Spectra‑Physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (for patents with effective filing date before March 16, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes items publicly known, used, offered for sale, or references (publications/patents) that disclose the claimed invention or elements of it. To be prior art, the item must have been made, known, used, published, or patented either before the invention was made (or an earlier inventor date) or more than one year before the filing date. Prior art does not include the inventor's own publication less than one year before the date of invention. Special limitations may apply under subsections of 35 U.S.C. §102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: statutory and case law; precise date rules and exceptions must be applied based on the patent's effective filing date and the applicable version of §102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) — claim invalid if present in single reference
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove anticipation (lack of novelty), alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that all requirements of the claim were present in a single previous device, method, printed publication, or patent (an 'anticipating prior art' reference). The prior art need not use the same words, but must disclose all claim elements either expressly or impliedly to a person of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation is determined claim‑by‑claim. Where the date of invention is disputed, jury must determine conception/reduction to practice and diligence. Authorities: applicable pre‑AIA §102 law; supporting cases and procedural guidance in instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of invention — conception, reduction to practice, and diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: If invention date is disputed, the factfinder must determine the date of invention. Date of invention is either when reduced to practice or when conceived (if the inventor was diligent in reducing to practice). Conception is the mental formation of a definite and permanent idea of the complete operative invention. Reduction to practice occurs when the invention has been constructed/used/tested sufficiently to show it works for its intended purpose or when a patent application is filed. Diligence requires continuous efforts (not necessarily daily).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception may be proven by drawings, disclosure to another, or other evidence beyond the inventor's testimony. Reduction to practice may be actual (prototype/test) or constructive (filed patent application). Authorities: cases cited in instructions concerning priority and conception/reduction/diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways a claim can be shown not new / patentee losing rights (enumerated grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of ways a patentee can lose rights or a claim be shown not new (choose applicable items based on contentions): (1) invention known or used by others in U.S. before date of invention; (2) already patented or described in printed publication anywhere in world before date of invention; (3) patentee's own patent/publication more than one year before effective filing date (statutory bars); (4) publicly used, sold, or offered for sale in U.S. more than one year before effective filing date; (5) abandonment of the invention; (6) foreign patent or application earlier than U.S. filing; (7) described in a published U.S. patent application or PCT application designated to U.S. by another before date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each item specifies a particular factual showing and date‑based rules; treat on claim‑by‑claim basis and apply pre‑AIA or AIA rules as appropriate to filing date.
